profile.summary: LucaVirus is a language model for viruses that reads both nucleotide sequences (DNA or RNA) and protein sequences in one model. It was trained on OpenVirus, a corpus of 15.7 million viral sequences, and outputs per-token and per-sequence embeddings. These embeddings are used, or the model is fine-tuned, for tasks such as viral sequence classification, protein fitness prediction and antibody-antigen binding prediction.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: LucaVirus is an encoder-only Transformer with about 1 billion parameters. It was initialised from the weights of LucaOne, a general biological foundation model, then reduced to 12 transformer layers with a context window of 3072 tokens. The default checkpoint's config gives hidden size 2560, 20 attention heads and one vocabulary for nucleotides and amino acids. Pretraining combines masked language modelling with seven supervised tasks. Three are sequence-level (order taxonomy for nucleotide and protein sequences, and UniProt functional keywords for proteins) and four are token-level (gene prediction on nucleotides, and homologous superfamily, conserved domain and active site annotation on proteins). The user tells the tokenizer whether an input is a gene (DNA or RNA) or a protein. In the paper, downstream tasks train a small head (attention pooling, a fully connected layer and a prediction head) on frozen LucaVirus embeddings.

sections.body: Five LucaVirus checkpoints are listed on Hugging Face under LucaGroup: default-step3.8M, prot-step3.8M, gene-step3.8M, mask-step1.4M and mask-step3.8M. The repository's training scripts describe the variants: one trained only with the masked language modelling task, one only on viral gene (DNA and RNA) data and one only on viral protein data. The repository's own embedding script downloads checkpoints from the authors' FTP server, while the Hugging Face checkpoints are loaded through the lucavirus package (version 1.1.1). A result should name the checkpoint and its revision; this page read the default checkpoint at revision 207da019. The README gives two figures for the LucaOne starting checkpoint: step 1,760,000 in its pretraining section and step=17600000 or 36000000 in its training scripts section. The paper says the pretrained weights, downstream models and training data are also on Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.15703216).

steps.title: Embed a nucleotide sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
import lucavirus
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel

model_id = "LucaGroup/LucaVirus-default-step3.8M"

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    trust_remote_code=True,
    force_download=True
)

model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    task_level="token_level",
    task_type="embedding",
    trust_remote_code=True,
    force_download=True
)

device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
model.to(device)
model.eval()

nucleotide_sequence = "ATGCGTACGTTAGC"
nucleotide_inputs = tokenizer(
    nucleotide_sequence,
    seq_type="gene",
    return_tensors="pt",
    add_special_tokens=True
)
new_nucleotide_inputs = {}
for item in nucleotide_inputs.items():
    new_nucleotide_inputs[item[0]] = item[1].to(device)
nucleotide_inputs = new_nucleotide_inputs

with torch.no_grad():
    nucleotide_outputs = model(**nucleotide_inputs)
    nucleotide_last_hidden = nucleotide_outputs.last_hidden_state
    mean_nucleotide_embedding = nucleotide_last_hidden[:, 1:-1, :].mean(dim=1)
print(f"Nucleotide Embedding Shape: {nucleotide_last_hidden.shape}")
print(mean_nucleotide_embedding)
PY

profile.summary: OpenSpliceAI predicts splice sites from DNA sequence. It is a PyTorch reimplementation of SpliceAI that scores every position as a donor site, an acceptor site or neither, and can also score how genetic variants change splicing. It ships a human model retrained on GRCh38 with MANE annotations, models for four other species, and tools to train new models.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: OpenSpliceAI keeps the SpliceAI design: a deep residual convolutional neural network that reads one-hot encoded DNA. In the 10,000 nt model the input passes through an initial Conv1D layer and 16 residual units with skip connections, then a softmax gives, for each position, the probability of donor, acceptor or neither. Smaller variants use fewer residual units (12 for 2000 nt, 8 for 400 nt). The input is padded with 5000 Ns on each side. For each flanking length five models were trained with different random seeds, and their outputs are averaged as an ensemble. The variant subcommand computes delta scores that measure how a variant changes splice site strength.

The authors strongly recommend the 10000 nt model; the others are for experimental and research use. Species models exist for mouse, zebrafish, honey bee and thale cress. The README at the commit read shows version v.0.0.7. A result should name the species model, the flanking length, whether the five-model ensemble or a single seed was used, and the package version.

profile.summary: RNA-km is a language model for non-coding RNA sequences, built to predict RNA secondary structure, including pseudoknots, without training on labelled structures. It reads a single RNA sequence and returns a 1024-value representation per nucleotide and attention maps. In the paper, the attention maps are turned into base pairs with a minimum-cost flow algorithm.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RNA-km is a transformer encoder with 12 layers and model width 1024; the code sets the feed-forward width to four times the model width and uses relative position biases instead of absolute positions. Its token vocabulary covers A, T, C, G and X; the script converts U to T and other letters to N. It was trained by self-supervision on 23 million ncRNA sequences, using a k-mer masking strategy. A pair head projects the per-nucleotide representations to pairwise features. For structure prediction the paper uses the attention maps with a minimum-cost flow algorithm; that algorithm is not part of the repository files read.

profile.summary: RNA-MSM is an RNA language model that reads a multiple sequence alignment (MSA) of a target RNA and its homologues rather than a single sequence. It outputs a per-nucleotide embedding and attention maps, which the authors use to predict RNA secondary structure (base pairs) and solvent accessibility. The MSA must first be built with a homology search tool such as RNAcmap3.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RNA-MSM follows the protein MSA Transformer design: an embedding module with two learned position embeddings, one for the rows (sequences in the MSA) and one for the columns (positions), then 10 transformer blocks with 12 attention heads each and a 768-dimensional embedding. The authors cut the block count from 12 to 10 because of GPU memory. It was trained with the BERT masked language modelling objective, masking 20% of MSA tokens. The 120 attention maps (10 blocks by 12 heads) and the embedding of the query sequence are the outputs; separate downstream networks in the repository turn them into secondary structure and solvent accessibility predictions.

sections.body: One pretrained checkpoint is released on Google Drive (RNA_MSM_pretrained.ckpt by the script's default path). The repository also carries trained downstream models for secondary structure and solvent accessibility, and the downstream datasets with their MSAs were released in July 2024. Results depend strongly on the MSA, so a result should name the checkpoint, the repository commit, and the homology search tool and settings used to build the MSA.

profile.summary: GenerRNA is a generative language model that writes new RNA sequences. It is a decoder-only transformer, the same style as GPT, trained on millions of natural RNA sequences so that it can sample sequences it has never seen. It takes no structure, label or alignment as input: either sample from it as it is, or fine-tune it on a family or a function first.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GenerRNA is a decoder-only transformer of 350 million parameters: 24 layers with a model dimension of 1280, the same shape as GPT-2-medium. It is trained to predict the next token, with no labels. Sequences are split by a byte-pair encoding tokenizer with a vocabulary of 1024, so one token covers several nucleotides. The context window is 1024 tokens, about 4000 nucleotides. In preprocessing, U was replaced with T and ambiguity codes were kept. Generation is sampling: sampling.py writes new sequences from a checkpoint and a tokenizer.

profile.summary: gLM2 is a genomic language model that reads a stretch of genome as a mixture of two alphabets: protein coding regions as amino acids, and the intergenic sequence between them as nucleotides. Each element is prefixed with a strand token. It is a transformer encoder trained by masked language modelling on the OMG metagenomic corpus, and the authors say its representations carry functional information as well as coevolutionary signals in protein-protein interfaces and genomic regulatory syntax.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: gLM2 is a transformer encoder trained with the masked language modelling objective. The input is a contig written as alternating coding and intergenic elements: coding elements as uppercase amino acids, intergenic elements as lowercase nucleotides, so the two alphabets cannot collide, and each element prefixed by <+> or <-> for the strand. The 650M checkpoint's config gives depth 33, dimension 1280, 20 heads, a SwiGLU feed-forward and a vocabulary of 37 tokens; the 150M checkpoint's config gives depth 30, dimension 640 and 10 heads. Pretraining used 315B tokens with a context length of 4096. An update in September 2024 raised the context from 2048 to 4096 tokens and changed intergenic tokenisation from BPE to per-nucleotide.

profile.summary: Sei is a deep learning model that reads a 4-kb human DNA sequence and predicts the probability of 21,907 chromatin profiles (transcription factor binding, histone marks and chromatin accessibility) at its centre. Those predictions are then summarised into 40 sequence classes, such as promoter, cell type-specific enhancer or Polycomb-repressed, which give a score for a sequence or for the effect of a variant.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results (model) and Methods; README: introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The Sei model has three parts: a convolutional network with parallel linear and nonlinear paths, residual dilated convolution layers that widen the receptive field without losing resolution, and a B-spline basis layer that reduces 256 spatial bins to 16 before fully connected output layers. It was trained with Selene in PyTorch as a multi-label classifier: for each 4-kb region, the label is whether the centre base overlaps a peak in each of the 21,907 profiles. The authors then predicted 30 million genome positions at a 100-bp step, reduced the predictions with PCA and clustered them with Louvain community detection. The 40 largest clusters are the sequence classes. A sequence's class score is a projection of its chromatin predictions onto each class vector; for variants the score is alt minus ref, with histone predictions adjusted for nucleosome occupancy.

The repository download script fetches it, with a resources archive holding hg19 and hg38 FASTA files. Whole-genome sequence class annotations for hg38, and for hg19 lifted over from hg38, are in a separate Zenodo record, and the authors recommend these annotations over raw sequence class scores for reference genome sequences. The training configuration is in train/train.yml. A result should name the repository commit and the Zenodo model record; this page read commit 1e16bff9.

profile.summary: NuFold predicts the full-atom 3D structure of a single RNA chain from its sequence. It takes the sequence, a multiple sequence alignment and a predicted secondary structure, and outputs ranked structure models as PDB files. It adapts the AlphaFold2 network to RNA, with a nucleobase-centred representation that lets the ribose ring take flexible shapes.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: NuFold keeps the three-part AlphaFold2 layout. An input module reads the sequence, an MSA from the rMSA pipeline and a secondary structure predicted by IPknot. Evoformer blocks embed the MSA and pairwise information. A structure module builds the 3D model, and the steps are repeated in recycling rounds to refine it. Instead of amino acids, the network uses seven letter types: the four nucleotides, unknown, gap and masked. The network predicts the translation and rotation of each base frame plus a set of torsion angles, which the nucleobase centre representation turns into full-atom coordinates. Training added self-distillation data from bpRNA-1m to the small set of PDB structures.

profile.summary: Optimus 5-Prime is a convolutional neural network that predicts how well a 5' UTR sequence drives translation, measured as mean ribosome load (MRL). It reads a one-hot encoded 5' UTR, 50 nucleotides in the main model, and outputs a single MRL value. It was trained on polysome profiling of 280,000 random 5' UTRs placed in front of an eGFP reporter, and the authors also used it with a genetic algorithm to design new 5' UTRs.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, Modeling 5' UTRs and ribosome loading; Fig. 2 legend

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The authors built a library of 280,000 reporter constructs with random 5' UTRs and a constant eGFP coding sequence and 3' UTR, measured ribosome loading by polysome profiling and RNA sequencing, and trained a CNN on 260,000 of them, holding out 20,000 for testing. The chosen architecture, from a 10-fold cross-validated grid search, has three convolution layers of 120 filters with filter length 8 and ReLU activation, a 40-node dense layer with 20% dropout, and one linear output. It was written in Python 2.7 with Keras on a TensorFlow backend and trained for three epochs. A separate model with the same layout predicts the full polysome profile, and a generalised version reads 5' UTRs of 25 to 100 nucleotides, zero-padded to 100.
sections.source_locator: Paper: MPRA design and validation; Online Methods, Convolution Neural Network, Polysome Profile Model, Generalized CNN

sections.body: The repository holds several saved Keras models in modeling/saved_models: the main MRL model (Figure 2), a retrained main model (Figure 4), a model for the genetic algorithm and its retrained version, and the polysome distribution model. The same folder also holds Varying_length_25to100_model.hdf5, whose name matches the paper's generalised 25 to 100 nucleotide model. Six further .h5 models (e1, e2, ep1, ep2, emp1, emp2) sit in modeling/cds_modification_comparisons/saved_data; the paper describes models trained on chemically modified RNA, but the sources read do not explain these file names. profile.summary: trRosettaRNA predicts the full-atom 3D structure of an RNA from its sequence. It takes a multiple sequence alignment and a secondary structure, uses a transformer network to predict inter-nucleotide distances, orientations and backbone torsion angles, and then folds a 3D model by energy minimisation in Rosetta. The output is a PDB file.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; package README: Overview, Usage

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: For a query RNA, an MSA is built (with rMSA, or Infernal against RNAcentral) and a secondary structure is predicted with SPOT-RNA. These are turned into an MSA representation and a pair representation, which also carries direct couplings from the MSA and the secondary structure probability matrix. A transformer called RNAformer, similar to the Evoformer in AlphaFold2, updates both representations. A single pass has 48 blocks, cycled 4 times. It outputs probability distributions for 1D torsion angles and 2D distances, contacts and orientations. These are converted into restraints that, with physics-based Rosetta energy terms, guide energy minimisation to full-atom models; the package generates several decoys and keeps the one with minimum energy.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Overview of trRosettaRNA; Methods, Preparation of input data, RNAformer, 3D structure folding; package README: Step 2

sections.body: Two releases of the standalone package are named. Version 1.0 is the version used in the Nature Communications paper, downloadable from the lab website. Version 1.1, on Zenodo (record 10616895, 2024-02-03), adds support for custom secondary structure files. The package ships one RNAformer checkpoint, params/model_1, used by default. For its benchmarks the paper trained separate models on date-filtered training sets to avoid leakage; those are not described as released. A result should name the package version, the MSA tool and database, and the secondary structure source, since the authors report sensitivity to secondary structure quality.

profile.summary: BMRetriever-7B is a biomedical text embedding model for dense retrieval. It turns a query (with a one-sentence task instruction) or a passage into a 4096-dimensional vector, and relevance is scored as the dot product between query and passage vectors. It is the largest of four BMRetriever models and is built on the BioMistral 7B language model, further trained on biomedical corpora and instruction data.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; README: Model Specifications, Model Usage; model card: Usage

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: BMRetriever starts from a pretrained language model (BioMistral for the 7B model), runs unsupervised pre-training on large biomedical corpora, then instruction fine-tuning on labelled datasets and synthetic pairs. At inference, each query is prefixed with a one-sentence task instruction, each passage with 'Represent this passage', and an end-of-sequence token is appended. The embedding is the final hidden state at the last token (last-token pooling). The 7B model is a 32-layer Mistral architecture with hidden size 4096.

The README reports the 7B model has the highest average scores of the four on the authors' retrieval tasks and applications. The instruction fine-tuning data, about 1.4M pairs, is released as BMRetriever/biomed_retrieval_dataset, and eval.py and prompt.py reproduce the BEIR experiments. prerequisites: Python with PyTorch and Hugging Face transformers installed; the sources give no install command. The config was saved with transformers 4.37.2.
A CUDA GPU: the example moves inputs to 'cuda'. Memory needs are not stated; the weights are float32 with 7,110,660,096 parameters.
Weights and code are MIT licensed; the weights are not gated.

steps.title: Embed and score example texts
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer

model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("BMRetriever/BMRetriever-7B") 
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("BMRetriever/BMRetriever-7B") 

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

from torch import Tensor
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel


def last_token_pool(last_hidden_states: Tensor,
                 attention_mask: Tensor) -> Tensor:
    last_hidden = last_hidden_states.masked_fill(~attention_mask[..., None].bool(), 0.0)
    left_padding = (attention_mask[:, -1].sum() == attention_mask.shape[0])
    if left_padding:
        embedding = last_hidden[:, -1]
    else:
        sequence_lengths = attention_mask.sum(dim=1) - 1
        batch_size = last_hidden.shape[0]
        embedding = last_hidden[torch.arange(batch_size, device=last_hidden.device), sequence_lengths]
    return embedding

def get_detailed_instruct_query(task_description: str, query: str) -> str:
    return f'{task_description}\nQuery: {query}'

def get_detailed_instruct_passage(passage: str) -> str:
    return f'Represent this passage\npassage: {passage}'

# Each query must come with a one-sentence instruction that describes the task
task = 'Given a scientific claim, retrieve documents that support or refute the claim'
queries = [
    get_detailed_instruct_query(task, 'Cis-acting lncRNAs control the expression of genes that are positioned in the vicinity of their transcription sites.'),
    get_detailed_instruct_query(task, 'Forkhead 0 (fox0) transcription factors are involved in apoptosis.')
]

# No need to add instruction for retrieval documents
documents = [
    get_detailed_instruct_passage("Gene regulation by the act of long non-coding RNA transcription Long non-protein-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are proposed to be the largest transcript class in the mouse and human transcriptomes. Two important questions are whether all lncRNAs are functional and how they could exert a function. Several lncRNAs have been shown to function through their product, but this is not the only possible mode of action. In this review we focus on a role for the process of lncRNA transcription, independent of the lncRNA product, in regulating protein-coding-gene activity in cis. We discuss examples where lncRNA transcription leads to gene silencing or activation, and describe strategies to determine if the lncRNA product or its transcription causes the regulatory effect."),
    get_detailed_instruct_passage("Noncoding transcription at enhancers: general principles and functional models. Mammalian genomes are extensively transcribed outside the borders of protein-coding genes. Genome-wide studies recently demonstrated that cis-regulatory genomic elements implicated in transcriptional control, such as enhancers and locus-control regions, represent major sites of extragenic noncoding transcription. Enhancer-templated transcripts provide a quantitatively small contribution to the total amount of cellular nonribosomal RNA; nevertheless, the possibility that enhancer transcription and the resulting enhancer RNAs may, in some cases, have functional roles, rather than represent mere transcriptional noise at accessible genomic regions, is supported by an increasing amount of experimental data. In this article we review the current knowledge on enhancer transcription and its functional implications.")
]
input_texts = queries + documents

max_length = 512

# Tokenize the input texts
batch_dict = tokenizer(input_texts, max_length=max_length-1, padding=True, truncation=True, return_tensors='pt')

# Important! Adding EOS token at the end
batch_dict['input_ids'] = [input_ids + [tokenizer.eos_token_id] for input_ids in batch_dict['input_ids']]
batch_dict = tokenizer.pad(batch_dict, padding=True, return_attention_mask=True, return_tensors='pt').to("cuda")

model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model(**batch_dict)
    embeddings = last_token_pool(outputs.last_hidden_state, batch_dict['attention_mask'])

scores = (embeddings[:2] @ embeddings[2:].T)
print(scores.tolist())
PY

profile.summary: OmniReg-GPT is a generative DNA foundation model for long human genomic sequences. It reads DNA tokenised into subword units and was pretrained to predict the next token on 20 kb windows of the human T2T genome. Its embeddings are fine-tuned for regulatory tasks such as histone marks, promoters and enhancers, gene expression, chromatin accessibility and 3D chromatin contacts, and it can generate candidate enhancer sequences from a prompt.

sections.body: OmniReg-GPT is a decoder-only transformer trained with next-token prediction. DNA is tokenised with the BPE tokenizer from GENA-LM (vocabulary 32,000). The network has 12 local blocks, where each window of tokens attends to itself and the preceding window, and 2 global blocks that build a whole-sequence representation. The authors say this reduces attention cost from quadratic to linear in sequence length. It uses rotary position embeddings and FlashAttention. For downstream tasks a single vector is taken as the mean of all token embeddings.

profile.summary: SpeciesLM is a family of species-aware DNA language models for the non-coding regions that flank genes. A model reads the sequence before the start codon or after the stop codon of a gene, together with a token naming the species it came from, and predicts masked nucleotides. The published models give per-nucleotide probabilities and sequence embeddings, which the authors use to find regulatory motifs and to predict gene expression and mRNA half-life. The original models were trained on fungi; a later metazoa checkpoint is the one TraitGym scores on human variants.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each model is a DNABERT transformer with 12 encoder blocks. Nucleotides are split into overlapping 6-mers before entering the model. During training, spans of overlapping 6-mers are masked and the model learns to reconstruct them by minimising cross-entropy. The species label is prepended to the sequence as an extra token whose embedding is learned. An agnostic version was trained without this token for comparison. To predict for a species not seen in training, the authors give the token of a closely related species (C. glabrata for the 3' model and K. africana for the 5' model). Sequence representations come from pooling hidden states; the tutorial notebook averages hidden layers from layer 8 onwards. The later metazoa checkpoint keeps the width, depth and head count but uses a rotary-embedding variant (model_type rotarybert) with its own modelling code loaded through trust_remote_code.

sections.body: Two sets of weights exist. The paper's fungal models are four branches of one Hugging Face repository: species and agnostic models for the 3' region (300 bp after the stop codon) and for the 5' region (1000 bp before the start codon plus the start codon). This page read downstream_species_lm at revision 742e7928 and upstream_species_lm at revision 1052abf2, taken from the branch listing. A second set is published under the johahi account: fungi upstream and downstream k1 models, a yeast start-site model, and specieslm-metazoa-upstream-k6, read here at revision 744863be. TraitGym scores that metazoa checkpoint with a 2000 bp window, so a result on this record should name the account, the checkpoint and the revision; the fungal and metazoa weights are not interchangeable. The upstream models were trained with FlashAttention and converted to standard Hugging Face models, which the README says may give slight numerical instabilities in float32.

profile.summary: ViroCaduceus is a DNA language model built by the ViroBench authors to test whether a virus-enriched pretraining corpus helps nucleotide models on viral tasks. It takes a Caduceus backbone and trains it on ViroBlend (also spelt ViroBland), a 216 Mbp mix of human, multi-species and viral sequence. Given a DNA sequence it returns hidden states, which the benchmark pools into embeddings for viral taxonomy and host classification.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ViroCaduceus uses the Caduceus (Mamba-DNA) architecture. The paper describes it as Caduceus-PS adapted with the same ViroBland pretraining used for the authors' ViroHyena models. The released file is a set of backbone weights. To use it, the demo script loads the Caduceus-Ph base model from kuleshov-group, then overlays the ViroCaduceus weights from pytorch_model.bin. It tokenises the sequence, takes the last hidden layer and mean-pools over non-special tokens to give one embedding per sequence. In ViroBench the backbone is frozen and a light supervised head is trained on top for classification.

Its sources disagree on the base: the paper says Caduceus-PS, while the model card and the demo script use Caduceus-Ph. profile.summary: Orca predicts the three-dimensional folding of the human genome from DNA sequence alone. It takes a genomic sequence of up to 256 Mb and returns predicted contact matrices at nine scales, from 4 kb resolution within 1 Mb up to whole-chromosome distances. It is used to run in silico Hi-C experiments: to ask what a structural variant, a haplotype or a designed sequence would do to local and large-scale genome structure.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: What is Orca, What can I use Orca for; paper: Results, Sequence-based prediction of multiscale 3D genome interactions

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Orca has a hierarchical sequence encoder and a cascade of decoders. The encoder turns a one-hot sequence into representations at nine resolutions, from 4 kb up to 1,024 kb. Each decoder predicts one 250 by 250 interaction matrix for a window of a given size, as a log fold change over a distance-based background. The decoders run from the top down: each lower level takes the sequence representation at its resolution, the prediction from the level above cropped and upsampled, and a pairwise distance encoding matrix. Encoder and decoders are convolutional with residual connections; each decoder has 112 convolution layers cycling through dilation factors 1 to 64. Predictions are symmetrised with their transpose and averaged between the forward and reverse-complement sequence. The encoder is also trained on an auxiliary task of predicting DNase-seq and ChIP-seq chromatin profiles.

A result should name the cell-type model and the scale, and the repository commit, since the weights come as Zenodo resource tarballs rather than from a versioned model hub. profile.summary: Akita predicts how a stretch of DNA folds in three dimensions. It takes just over one megabase of sequence, one-hot encoded, and returns a predicted contact map for that window, as log observed over expected values, for each of five cell types it was trained on. It is used for in silico work: saturation mutagenesis, interpreting eQTLs, predicting the effect of structural variants and comparing species.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Akita is a convolutional network in two halves. A 1D trunk reads the one-hot sequence: a convolution block, then a tower of ten convolution and pooling blocks, then eight dilated residual blocks, which brings 1,048,576 bases down to 2,048 bp bins. A 2D head turns the 1D representation into a pairwise map (one_to_two with a mean operation), concatenates a distance encoding, symmetrises it, applies six dilated 2D residual blocks, crops the edges and reads off the upper triangle with a diagonal offset of 2. The final layer has five linear units, one per training dataset. Training used mean squared error with SGD, batch size 2, and reverse-complement and shift augmentation. The published model has 751,653 parameters, of which 746,149 are trainable.

python - <<'PY'
import json, os, subprocess
os.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = '-1' ### run on CPU
import numpy as np
import pysam
from basenji import dna_io, seqnn

with open('params.json') as params_open:
    params = json.load(params_open)
    params_model = params['model']

seqnn_model = seqnn.SeqNN(params_model)
seqnn_model.restore('model_best.h5')
print('successfully loaded')

os.makedirs('./data', exist_ok=True)
if not os.path.isfile('./data/hg38.ml.fa'):
    print('downloading hg38.ml.fa')
    subprocess.call('curl -o ./data/hg38.ml.fa.gz https://storage.googleapis.com/basenji_barnyard2/hg38.ml.fa.gz', shell=True)
    subprocess.call('gunzip ./data/hg38.ml.fa.gz', shell=True)

fasta_open = pysam.Fastafile('./data/hg38.ml.fa')
seq = fasta_open.fetch('chr12', 115163136, 116211712).upper()
seq_1hot = dna_io.dna_1hot(seq)
test_pred_from_seq = seqnn_model.model.predict(np.expand_dims(seq_1hot,0))
print(test_pred_from_seq.shape)
PY

profile.summary: BulkFormer is a family of foundation models for human bulk RNA-seq. A model takes one expression profile per sample, covering about twenty thousand protein-coding genes, and returns either a single vector that represents the whole sample or a vector per gene plus recovered expression values. Those vectors are then used as frozen features for downstream prediction, for example disease classification, prognosis or drug response.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The two current models work differently. Atlas gives each gene a token that combines a learned identity embedding with a linear projection of log2(TPM + 1), then passes a CLS token and up to 4,096 selected gene tokens through 16 bidirectional transformer blocks of width 1,024 with 16 heads and SwiGLU feed-forward layers; the sample feature is the 1,024-dimensional CLS output taken before the projection head. Latest encodes all 19,973 gene positions at once: gene identity, a sinusoidal encoding of expression and a global expression MLP (19,973 to 2,560 to 768) are normalised separately and summed with fixed 1:1:1 coefficients, then a residual weighted graph convolution of hidden width 256 feeds a 12-layer Performer of width 768. A small network reads how much of the input is missing and applies a bounded gain and offset to the expression head.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three generations sit in one repository. The publication family has five sizes: 37M, 50M, 93M, 127M and 147M parameters, with the authors recommending 147M where resources allow. The 2026-11-04 release added BulkFormer-Atlas (242.37M) and BulkFormer-Latest (154.55M), and on 2026-11-06 Latest moved to its final epoch-20 checkpoint. Each new model carries an immutable checkpoint ID: atlas-infonce-epoch10-update320000 and latest-20261106-epoch20-update148300. The repository is explicit that published PRIMO scores were produced by earlier checkpoints: Atlas appears as BulkFormer-variant, and the epoch-19 Latest as BulkFormer-V3Plus, whose scores do not evaluate the current download. A result should name the model, the checkpoint ID and the pooling protocol.

profile.summary: BulkRNABert is a transformer language model for bulk RNA-seq data. It takes the expression levels of a fixed set of genes from one sample and returns embeddings of that sample. The embeddings are used to build downstream models for cancer-type classification and survival-time prediction.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: BulkRNABert is an encoder-only transformer. Each gene in the input is one token, and its expression value is binned and embedded together with a gene embedding. During pretraining, expression values are masked at random and the model learns to reconstruct them from the other genes, as in BERT. The released configuration has 4 transformer layers, an embedding size of 256, 8 attention heads, 64 expression bins and 19,062 genes. For a downstream task the authors either probe the learned embeddings or use parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

It also ships a classification model for five TCGA cohorts used in an example notebook. The Hugging Face repository InstaDeepAI/BulkRNABert holds a PyTorch version for the transformers library, described as pretrained on TCGA, plus the JAX parameters. steps.title: Compute embeddings for the sample data
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import haiku as hk
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import pandas as pd

from multiomics_open_research.bulk_rna_bert.pretrained import get_bulkrnabert_pretrained_model
from multiomics_open_research.common.preprocess import preprocess_omic

# Get pretrained model
parameters, forward_fn, tokenizer, config = get_bulkrnabert_pretrained_model(
    model_name="bulk_rna_bert_tcga",
    embeddings_layers_to_save=(4,),
    checkpoint_directory="checkpoints/",
)
forward_fn = hk.transform(forward_fn)

# Get bulk RNASeq data and tokenize it
gene_expression_df = pd.read_csv("data/bulkrnabert/tcga_sample.csv")
gene_expression_array = preprocess_omic(gene_expression_df, config)
gene_expression_ids = tokenizer.batch_tokenize(gene_expression_array)
gene_expression_ids = jnp.asarray(gene_expression_ids, dtype=jnp.int32)

# Inference
random_key = jax.random.PRNGKey(0)
outs = forward_fn.apply(parameters, random_key, gene_expression_ids)

# Get mean embeddings from layer 4
gene_expression_mean_embeddings = outs["embeddings_4"].mean(axis=1)
PY

profile.summary: Enigma is a sequence-to-function model for regulatory genomics from Deep Genomics. It reads a long stretch of DNA and predicts genome tracks such as RNA-seq, DNase-seq and ATAC-seq signal at single-base resolution. Enigma-Distilled is the released pretrained checkpoint, a distilled model provided for non-commercial use.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Enigma takes a one-hot DNA sequence and predicts many genome tracks at once, with a separate output head for human (hg38) and mouse (mm10). The default configuration in the code combines a U-Net with 7 downsampling steps and an 8-layer transformer of width 1536 that uses rotary position embeddings and FlashAttention, with prediction resolution 1. The authors' stated aim was efficiency: a smaller, curated set of training tracks and a cheaper architecture rather than a larger model. The released checkpoint is a distilled model, which GUANinE v1.1 describes as ensemble-distilled. The distillation procedure itself was not in the sources read.

profile.summary: hgT5 is a set of T5 transformer models pretrained on the human genome by the authors of the GUANinE benchmark. The models read DNA sequences of about 512 bp, split into learned tokens, and were fine-tuned separately on each GUANinE task, such as chromatin accessibility, sequence conservation and yeast promoter expression. They were built to test how self-supervised pretraining helps on these tasks.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: hgT5 uses the T5 encoder-decoder transformer at 770 M parameters. DNA is split into tokens with a unigram language model tokenizer, with vocabularies of 512+3, 2048+3 or 8192+3 tokens. The models were pretrained on the human genome with T5's span-corruption objective, using 15% noise density and a mean span length of 3 tokens, then fine-tuned on each benchmark task separately. Matching T5 models without pretraining were trained as a comparison.

sections.title: Pretraining corpus
sections.body: The pretraining corpus is a reduced copy of hg38. The authors removed N-rich and repeat-rich regions and near-duplicate segments, which left 1.64 Gbp. They then made upsampled versions in which minor alleles from 1000 Genomes Project Phase 3 (allele frequency 1e-3 or greater) were inserted at random, to reduce reference bias.

sections.body: Three hgT5 models exist, named by vocabulary size: hgT5-515, hgT5-2051 and hgT5-8195. The authors trained three pretraining replicates of each and kept two. Each was then fine-tuned per task, so a published score refers to a task-specific fine-tuned model. GUANinE v1.1 re-reports hgT5-8195. profile.summary: Puffin-D is a deep learning model that predicts transcription initiation signals from DNA sequence. It takes 100 kbp of genome sequence and returns base-level predictions for ten tracks: five assays that map transcription start sites (FANTOM CAGE, ENCODE CAGE, ENCODE RAMPAGE, GRO-cap and PRO-cap) on each strand. It is the prediction-focused companion of Puffin, an interpretable model from the same authors.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction; Puffin-D

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Puffin-D is a fully convolutional network. One-hot DNA passes through a stack of strided 1D convolutions that downsample the sequence by factors of 4, 4, 5, 5, 5 and 2, each followed by residual convolution blocks. Upsampling layers with skip connections then restore base resolution. This down-and-up pass is repeated a second time. A final 1x1 convolution with a softplus gives 10 non-negative output tracks at each position. Training details were not in the sources read.

sections.title: Puffin and Puffin-D
sections.body: The repository holds two models. Puffin is an interpretation-focused model that explains each transcription start site in terms of motifs and single bases, and works on short sequences with 325 bp padding on each side. Puffin-D is the deep learning model for prediction over 100 kbp. The README says Puffin-D gives better predictions when prediction is the main need.

profile.summary: DeepFoldRNA predicts the 3D (tertiary) structure of an RNA from its sequence alone. It builds a multiple sequence alignment and secondary structure prediction for the input RNA, uses a deep self-attention network to predict distance and angle restraints, and then folds the chain by gradient-based simulation. The output is all-atom models in PDB format, before and after refinement.
profile.summary_source_locator: bioRxiv abstract; README.txt: Running instructions

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The pipeline has four stages. First, rMSA builds an MSA and PETfold predicts secondary structure; SPOT-RNA-1D predicts torsion angles. Second, a neural network with 48 MSA transformer blocks, 4 single-sequence blocks and 2 pair blocks, run for 4 recycling cycles, predicts restraints: binned distances from 2 to 40 Angstrom, inter-residue orientation angles and torsion angles. Third, gradient-based folding simulations build the structure from these restraints. Fourth, SimRNA and QRNAS refine the full-atom model. The authors note that the restraints do not include base atoms, so the unrefined model has slightly better backbone RMSD but worse base pairing than the refined one.

strengths.text: Needs only the RNA sequence as input; the MSA and secondary structure are generated by the pipeline.
The authors report an average RMSD of 2.69 Angstrom and TM-score of 0.743 on Rfam and RNA-Puzzles benchmarks, and about 1 minute to fold a medium-sized RNA. These are the authors' own figures.
Each stage can be run on its own (input generation, restraint prediction, folding, refinement), which helps reuse of precomputed MSAs.

limitations.text: The sequence databases for MSA generation need more than 500 GB of disk and hours to download; the program needs an x86_64 Linux machine.
Non-commercial licence per the README, with a conflicting MIT LICENSE file; several third-party tools (PETfold, rMSA, SimRNA, QRNAS, SPOT-RNA-1D) have their own licences.
The unrefined model has worse base pairing because the restraints do not cover base atoms, and refinement can introduce chain breaks.
Single-chain RNA only, with standard bases A, G, C and U; the sources describe no complexes or modified nucleotides.

profile.summary: DRfold predicts the 3D (tertiary) structure of an RNA from its nucleotide sequence alone, without a multiple sequence alignment. Deep learning models trained on solved RNA structures predict both coarse nucleotide positions and inter-nucleotide geometry; these are combined into an energy function that guides structure assembly. The output is a refined all-atom model in PDB format.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods: Feature preparation and embedding; README: Example

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DRfold encodes the sequence as one-hot vectors (A, U, G, C and N for unknown) and adds secondary structure predicted by RNAfold and PETfold as pair features. A stack of 48 transformer blocks, extended from AlphaFold2's Evoformer, updates sequence and pair representations, with 3 recycles. Two kinds of model are trained. End-to-end models use a structure module with invariant point attention to place each nucleotide as a rigid three-bead unit (C4', P and glycosidic N). Geometry models predict inter-nucleotide geometry restraints. Both outputs are combined into a hybrid energy potential that is minimised to assemble a coarse-grained structure. Arena rebuilds full atoms and OpenMM refines the model.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Feature preparation and embedding; RNA transformer network; RNA structure module); Results on refinement

sections.title: Training data
sections.body: The training set holds 3864 unique RNAs from the PDB deposited before 2021. Test structures deposited in or after 2021, and their sequence cluster members, were excluded from training. Training crops were limited to under 200 nucleotides because of GPU memory (a single Nvidia A40 GPU). The training and test sets are available for download from the authors' website.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results (benchmark set description); Discussion of large RNAs

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The GitHub repository does not include the trained models; they are downloaded separately as DRfold_models.zip from the Zhang group website. A run uses 6 end-to-end models and 3 geometry models; the final model is DPR.pdb. A result should name the repository commit (this page read 9586990c) and the date the model archive was downloaded, since the archive has no version number in the sources read.

Training and test sets are separated by deposition date and sequence clustering, and both sets can be downloaded.
